chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said:
I asked Abā al-Hasan عليه السلام about wearing al-firā’, al-sammūr, al-fanak, foxes, and all skins. He said: “There is no problem with that.”

So these two reports are to be understood as applying to the state of taqiyyah, because they also include mention of foxes, and we have already clarified that it is among those things in which salat is not permissible. As for al-sinjāb specifically, salat in it has been permitted for us, and we have already explained that. And as for al-sammūr, we have already clarified in the hadith of Zurārah and others that it is among those things in which salat is not permissible, and this gives it further clarification.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary conformity in circumstances of risk
key_terms.الثَّعَالِبِ: foxes; here referring to fox fur or skins used as clothing
key_terms.السَّمُّورُ: sable or a similar fur-bearing animal; stated here as not permissible for salat
key_terms.السِّنْجَابُ: squirrel fur; mentioned here as specifically permitted for salat
key_terms.الصَّلَاةُ: salat; the ritual prayer whose validity is being discussed
key_terms.الْجُلُودِ: skins or hides used as garments

ai.seo_question: Can one perform salat in garments made from squirrel, sable, fox, or other animal furs according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This report discusses the legal ruling on wearing and praying in garments made from certain animal furs and skins. The apparent permissive report is explained as being under taqiyyah because it includes fox fur, while other reports clarify that salat is not valid in some of these materials, with an exception noted for al-sinjāb.
